stem_tex: The slope of the curve $y^3 - xy^2 = 16$ at the point where $y=2$ is
explanation_tex: At $y=2$, $8-4x=16$ gives $x=-2$. Implicit differentiation gives $(3y^2-2xy)y'=y^2$, so $y'=4/(12+8)=1/5$.

stem_tex: The slope of the curve $y^2 - xy - 5x = 1$ at the point $(0,-1)$ is
explanation_tex: Implicit differentiation gives $(2y-x)y'=y+5$. At $(0,-1)$, $y'=4/(-2)=-2$.

stem_tex: Find an equation of the tangent to $y=x\cos2x$ at $(\pi/4,0)$.
explanation_tex: $y\prime=\cos2x-2x\sin2x$. At $x=\pi/4$, $y=0$ and $y\prime=-\pi/2$. The tangent is $y=-\frac\pi2(x-\frac\pi4)$.
resolved_source_issue: The stated point is not on the curve: at $x=\pi/4$, $x\cos2x=0$, not $\pi/4$. The actual tangent there is $y=-\frac\pi2(x-\frac\pi4)$, and none of the choices gives it.
source_correction: Corrected the point to (pi/4,0) and supplied the corresponding tangent as option A.

stem_tex: The tangent to the curve of $y = xe^{-2x}$ is horizontal when $x$ is equal to
explanation_tex: Differentiate: $y'=e^{-2x}(1-2x)$. Since the exponential never vanishes, the horizontal tangent occurs at $x=1/2$.

stem_tex: The minimum value of the slope of the curve $y = x^5 + 2x^3 - 3x$ is
explanation_tex: The slope is $5x^4+6x^2-3\ge-3$, with equality at $x=0$.

stem_tex: An equation of the tangent to the hyperbola $x^2-y^2=20$ at the point $(6,4)$ on the curve is
explanation_tex: Implicit differentiation gives $2x-2y\,y\prime=0$, so the slope at $(6,4)$ is $3/2$. Thus $y-4=\frac32(x-6)$, or $y=\frac32x-5$, choice C.
resolved_source_issue: Implicit differentiation gives $y'=x/y=3/2$. The tangent is $y-4=\frac32(x-6)$, or $y=\frac32x-5$. Options A and C are the same line, so the item has two correct choices.
source_correction: Changed duplicate option A to a different line; retained the correct tangent in C.

stem_tex: A tangent to the curve $y^2-xy+16=0$ is vertical when
explanation_tex: Differentiate to get $(2y-x)y'=y$. A vertical tangent has $x=2y$ with $y\ne0$. Substitution into the curve yields $16-y^2=0$, so $y=\pm4$.

stem_tex: The volume of a sphere is given by $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$. Use a tangent line to approximate the increase in volume, in cubic inches, when the radius of a sphere is increased from 4 to 4.1 inches.
explanation_tex: The differential is $dV=4\pi r^2dr$. At $r=4$ and $dr=0.1$, $dV=4\pi(16)(0.1)=6.4\pi$ cubic inches.

stem_tex: When $x=4$, the equation $2x^2-y^3=24$ has the solution $y=2$. Using a tangent line to the graph of the curve, approximate $y$ when $x=4.03$.
explanation_tex: Implicit differentiation gives $y'=4x/(3y^2)=4/3$ at $(4,2)$. Thus $y\approx2+(4/3)(0.03)=2.04$.

stem_tex: If the side $e$ of a square is increased by 2%, then the area is increased approximately
explanation_tex: Since $A=e^2$, $dA=2e\,de$. A 2% side increase gives $de=0.02e$, so $dA=0.04e^2$.

stem_tex: The edge of a cube has length 20 in., with a possible error of 2%. The possible error, in cubic inches, in the volume of the cube is
explanation_tex: Using differentials, $dV=3e^2de=3(20)^2(0.02\cdot20)=480$ cubic inches. This is the approximate propagated error; the exact upper error is $20.4^3-20^3=489.664$.

stem_tex: The function $f(x) = x^4 - 8x^2$ has
choices_tex: one local minimum and two local maxima
one local minimum and no local maximum
no local minimum and one local maximum
two local minima and one local maximum
explanation_tex: Factor $f'=4x(x-2)(x+2)$. Its signs on the four intervals are $-,+,-,+$, giving minima at $x=\pm2$ and a maximum at $0$.

stem_tex: The number of inflection points on the graph of $f(x) = x^4 - 8x^2$ is
explanation_tex: The second derivative is $f''=12x^2-16$, which changes sign at $x=\pm2/\sqrt3$. There are two inflection points.

stem_tex: The maximum value of the function $y = -6\sqrt{3-x}$ is
explanation_tex: The real domain is $x\le3$. Since $\sqrt{3-x}\ge0$, $y\le0$, and $y=0$ at $x=3$.

stem_tex: The total number of local maximum and minimum points of the function whose derivative, for all $x$, is given by $f'(x) = x(x-4)^2(x+2)^4$ is
explanation_tex: The even-power factors do not change sign at $-2$ or $4$. The sign of $f'$ changes only at $x=0$, from negative to positive, so there is one local extremum.

stem_tex: For which curve shown below are both $f'$ and $f''$ negative?
explanation_tex: A negative first derivative means the graph decreases; a negative second derivative means its slopes become more negative. Curve A is decreasing and concave down.

figure.alt: Four curves labeled A through D.

stem_tex: For which curve shown below is $f\prime\prime$ positive but $f\prime$ negative?
explanation_tex: Curve B decreases while its slopes become less negative as $x$ increases. Hence $f'<0$ and $f''>0$.

figure.alt: Four curves labeled A through D.

stem_tex: The position of a particle moving along a horizontal line is $s=t^3-9t^2+27t-5$. The object is moving to the right for
explanation_tex: Differentiate $s$: $v=3t^2-18t+27=3(t-3)^2$. This is positive except at $t=3$, so the particle moves right at all other times.

stem_tex: The position of a particle moving along a horizontal line is $s=t^3-9t^2+27t-5$. The minimum value of the speed is
explanation_tex: Speed is $|v|=3(t-3)^2\ge0$, attaining its minimum $0$ at $t=3$.

stem_tex: The position of a particle moving along a horizontal line is $s=t^3-9t^2+27t-5$. The acceleration is positive
explanation_tex: Acceleration is $a=v'=6t-18=6(t-3)$, which is positive exactly when $t>3$.

stem_tex: The position of a particle moving along a horizontal line is $s=t^3-9t^2+27t-5$. The speed of the particle is decreasing for
explanation_tex: Away from $t=3$, $v>0$, so speed decreases when $a=6(t-3)<0$, namely $t<3$.

stem_tex: A particle moves along a horizontal line with position $s=t^4-10t^3+36t^2+3$ at time $t$. The particle is at rest when $t$ is equal to
explanation_tex: Velocity is $v=4t^3-30t^2+72t=2t(2t^2-15t+36)$. The quadratic has discriminant $225-288<0$ and is always positive. Thus only $t=0$ gives rest.
source_correction: The stated polynomial has only one zero of velocity, t=0.

stem_tex: A particle moves along a horizontal line with position $s=t^4-10t^3+36t^2+3$ at time $t$. The velocity, $v$, is increasing when
explanation_tex: Acceleration is $a=12t^2-60t+72=12(t-2)(t-3)$. Velocity increases where $a>0$: $t<2$ or $t>3$.

stem_tex: A particle moves along a horizontal line with position $s=t^4-10t^3+36t^2+3$ at time $t$. The speed of the particle is increasing for
explanation_tex: The quadratic factor in $v=2t(2t^2-15t+36)$ is positive, so $v$ has the sign of $t$. Combining this with $a=12(t-2)(t-3)$, velocity and acceleration share a sign on $(0,2)$ and $(3,\infty)$.

stem_tex: The displacement from the origin of a particle moving on a line is given by $s = 2t^4-8t^3$. The maximum displacement during the time interval $-2 \leq t \leq 4$ is
explanation_tex: Critical times satisfy $s'=8t^2(t-3)=0$, so check $-2,0,3,4$. The positions are $96,0,-54,0$, respectively. The maximum is $96$.

stem_tex: If a particle moves along a line according to the law $s = t^5+10t^4$, then the number of times it reverses direction is
explanation_tex: Velocity is $v=5t^3(t+8)$. Its sign changes at both $t=-8$ and $t=0$, so over all real times there are two reversals. If time were restricted to $t\ge0$, there would be none; no such restriction is stated.

stem_tex: The position vector of a moving point is $\mathbf R(t)=\langle4\cos(\pi t/4),3\sin(\pi t/4)\rangle$. A single equation in $x$ and $y$ for the path of the point is
explanation_tex: From $x=4\cos(\pi t/4)$ and $y=3\sin(\pi t/4)$, $x^2/16+y^2/9=1$, equivalently $9x^2+16y^2=144$.

stem_tex: The position vector of a moving point is $\mathbf R(t)=\langle4\cos(\pi t/4),3\sin(\pi t/4)\rangle$. When $t=4$, the speed of the particle is
explanation_tex: Velocity is $\langle-\pi\sin(\pi t/4),(3\pi/4)\cos(\pi t/4)\rangle$. At $t=4$ it is $\langle0,-3\pi/4\rangle$, with speed $3\pi/4$.

stem_tex: The position vector of a moving point is $\mathbf R(t)=\langle4\cos(\pi t/4),3\sin(\pi t/4)\rangle$. The magnitude of the acceleration when $t=4$ is
explanation_tex: Acceleration is $\langle-(\pi^2/4)\cos(\pi t/4),-(3\pi^2/16)\sin(\pi t/4)\rangle$. At $t=4$ its magnitude is $\pi^2/4$.

stem_tex: The position vector of a moving point is $\mathbf R(t)=\langle4\cos(\pi t/4),3\sin(\pi t/4)\rangle$. At the point where $t=1$, the slope of the curve along which the particle moves is
explanation_tex: The slope is $(dy/dt)/(dx/dt)=-(3/4)\cot(\pi t/4)$. At $t=1$, it equals $-3/4$.

stem_tex: A balloon is being filled with helium at the rate of 8 ft$^3$/min. The rate, in square feet per minute, at which the surface area is increasing when the volume is $\dfrac{32\pi}{3}$ ft$^3$ is
explanation_tex: For a spherical balloon, $V=4\pi r^3/3=32\pi/3$ gives $r=2$. Since $A=4\pi r^2$, $dA/dV=2/r=1$, so $dA/dt=8$ square feet per minute.

stem_tex: A circular conical reservoir, vertex down, has depth 30 ft and radius at the top 15 ft. Water is leaking out so that the surface is falling at the rate of $\dfrac{1}{3}$ ft/hr. The rate, in cubic feet per hour, at which the water is leaving the reservoir when the water is 6 ft deep is
explanation_tex: Similar triangles give $r=h/2$, so $V=\pi h^3/12$ and $V'=\pi h^2h'/4$. With $h=6$, $h'=-1/3$, $V'=-3\pi$; the outflow magnitude is $3\pi$.

stem_tex: A local minimum value of the function $y = \dfrac{e^x}{3x}$ is
explanation_tex: Differentiate to get $y'=e^x(x-1)/(3x^2)$. It changes from negative to positive at $x=1$, so the local minimum value is $e/3$.

stem_tex: The area of the largest rectangle that can be drawn with one side along the $x$-axis and two vertices on the curve of $y = e^{-2x^2}$ is
explanation_tex: The rectangle has width $2x$ and height $e^{-2x^2}$, so $A=2xe^{-2x^2}$ for $x>0$. Its derivative is $2e^{-2x^2}(1-4x^2)$, changing from positive to negative at $x=1/2$. The maximum area is $e^{-1/2}=\sqrt{1/e}$.

stem_tex: A line with a negative slope is drawn through the point $(2,3)$ forming a right triangle with the positive $x$- and $y$-axes. The slope of the line forming the triangle of least area is
explanation_tex: Write the slope as $-k$, $k>0$. The intercepts are $2+3/k$ and $3+2k$, giving area $6+2k+9/(2k)$. Its derivative vanishes at $k=3/2$ and changes from negative to positive. Thus the slope is $-3/2$.

stem_tex: The point(s) on the curve $x^2-y^2=9$ closest to the point $(10,0)$ is (are)
explanation_tex: Using $y^2=x^2-9$, the squared distance is $(x-10)^2+y^2=2(x-5)^2+41$. Its minimum occurs at $x=5$, where $y=\pm4$.

stem_tex: The sum of the squares of two positive numbers is 300; their minimum product is
explanation_tex: Both numbers must be positive, so their product is positive. Taking one arbitrarily close to $0$ makes the product approach $0$, but never attain it. The infimum is $0$ and there is no minimum.

stem_tex: The first-quadrant point on the curve $y^2x = 64$ that is closest to the point $(2,0)$ is
explanation_tex: With $y^2=64/x$, minimize $D^2=(x-2)^2+64/x$ on $x>0$. Its derivative is $2(x-2)-64/x^2$, zero at $x=4$. Since the second derivative is $2+128/x^3>0$, this is the unique minimum, giving $y=4$.

stem_tex: If $h$ is a small negative number, then the local linear approximation for $\sqrt[3]{64+h}$ is
If $f(x) = xe^{-2x}$, then at $x=0$
explanation_tex: The derivative is $f'(x)=e^{-2x}(1-2x)$, so $f'(0)=1>0$ and $f$ is increasing near $0$.

stem_tex: A function $f$ has a derivative for each $x$ such that $|x|<3$ and has a local minimum at $(3,-7)$. Which statement below must be true?
choices_tex: none of the preceding is necessarily true
explanation_tex: Differentiability is guaranteed only for $|x|<3$, not at $3$. For example, $f(x)=|x-3|-7$ has the required minimum but no derivative there. A local minimum alone also does not impose the global derivative signs in C.

stem_tex: The height of a rectangular box is 10 in. Its length increases at the rate of 3 in./sec; its width decreases at the rate of 5 in./sec. When the length is 6 in. and the width is 9 in., the rate, in cubic inches per second, at which the volume of the box is changing is
explanation_tex: With fixed height $10$, $V=10lw$, so $V'=10(l'w+lw')=10(3\cdot9+6(-5))=-30$ cubic inches per second.

stem_tex: The tangent to the curve $x^3+x^2y+5y=17$ at the point $(2,1)$ has slope
If $f(x) = ax^6+bx^2$ and $ab>0$, then
choices_tex: the curve has no horizontal tangents
the curve is concave up for all $x$
the curve has no inflection point
none of the preceding is necessarily true
explanation_tex: Since $ab>0$, $a$ and $b$ have the same nonzero sign. Then $f''=30ax^4+2b$ always has that sign and never changes concavity, so there is no inflection point.

stem_tex: A function $f$ is continuous and differentiable on the interval $[0,4]$, where $f'$ is positive but $f''$ is negative. Which table could represent points on $f$?
explanation_tex: For equal $x$ steps, increasing and strictly concave-down values have positive, decreasing secant slopes. Only C has successive increases $8,6,4,2$.

stem_tex: An equation of the tangent to the curve with parametric equations $x = 3t+1$, $y = 4-t^3$ at the point where $t=1$ is
Given the function $f(x) = \sqrt[3]{x}$, it is known that $f(125) = 5$. Using the tangent line to the graph of $f(x)$, approximately how much less than 5 is $\sqrt[3]{124}$?
explanation_tex: At $x=125$, $f'(125)=1/(3\cdot25)=1/75$. Decreasing $x$ by $1$ decreases the tangent-line estimate by $1/75$.

stem_tex: The best linear approximation for $f(x) = \cot x$ near $x = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ is $y=$
Given $f(x) = e^{kx}$, approximate $f(h)$, where $h$ is near zero, using a tangent-line approximation. $f(h) \approx$
explanation_tex: Since $f(0)=1$ and $f'(0)=k$, the tangent approximation is $f(h)\approx1+kh$.

stem_tex: If $f(x) = cx^2+dx+e$ for the function shown in the graph, then
explanation_tex: The graph is concave down, so $f''=2c<0$. Its slope at $0$ is negative, so $d=f'(0)<0$, and the positive vertical intercept gives $e=f(0)>0$.

figure.alt: Decreasing concave-down quadratic with positive vertical intercept.

stem_tex: Given $f(x) = \log_{10}x$ and $\log_{10}(104) \approx 2.0170$, which is closest to $f'(100)$?
explanation_tex: Use the nearby secant: $f'(100)\approx(2.0170-2)/4=0.00425$, closest to $0.0043$. The exact derivative is $1/(100\ln10)\approx0.004343$.

stem_tex: The point on the curve $y = \sqrt{3x-2}$ at which the tangent is parallel to the line $3x-8y=10$ is
explanation_tex: The line has slope $3/8$. Setting $3/(2\sqrt{3x-2})=3/8$ gives $\sqrt{3x-2}=4$, hence $x=6$ and $y=4$.

stem_tex: An equation of the tangent to the curve $x^2 = 6y$ at the point on the curve where $x=-3$ is
explanation_tex: At $x=-3$, $y=x^2/6=3/2$ and $y'=x/3=-1$. The tangent is $y-3/2=-(x+3)$, equivalent to $2x+2y+3=0$.

stem_tex: The table shows the velocity at time $t$ of an object moving along a line. Estimate the acceleration (in ft/sec$^2$) at $t=6$ sec. $\begin{array}{c|rrrr}t\ (\mathrm{sec})&0&4&8&10\\v\ (\mathrm{ft/sec})&24&20&12&0\end{array}$
explanation_tex: Estimate acceleration by the centered secant through $t=4,8$: $(12-20)/(8-4)=-2$ ft/sec$^2$.

stem_tex: The figure shows $f\prime$ on $[0,8]$. From the graph it follows that
explanation_tex: The graph is of $f'$, which is positive between $1$ and $2$. Therefore $f$ increases there and $f(1)<f(2)$.

figure.alt: Graph of f prime on [0,8], constant to x=3 then decreasing.

stem_tex: The figure shows $f\prime$ on $[0,8]$. Which statement best describes $f$ at $x=5$?
choices_tex: $f$ is increasing and concave down near $x=5$.
explanation_tex: Near $x=5$, $f\prime>0$ and $f\prime$ is decreasing. Therefore $f$ is increasing and concave down. The derivative does not vanish or change sign there, and its slope does not change sign, so there is no extremum or inflection point.

figure.alt: Graph of f prime on [0,8], constant to x=3 then decreasing.

resolved_source_issue: At $x=5$ the displayed derivative is positive and decreasing. Thus $f$ is increasing and concave down there, with neither an extremum nor a change of concavity. Its value is unknown, so a root is not implied. None of the listed statements follows.
source_correction: Replaced the unsupported inflection-point option with the behavior shown by the derivative graph.

stem_tex: The figure shows $f\prime$ on $[0,8]$. For which interval is the graph of $f$ concave downward?
explanation_tex: The derivative graph is strictly decreasing throughout $(3,8)$, so $f''<0$ and $f$ is concave down on that full interval. B and C are also subintervals of concavity; D is the maximal interval among the choices.

figure.alt: Graph of f prime on [0,8], constant to x=3 then decreasing.

source_correction: D gives the maximal interval; B and C also lie within the same concave-down interval.

stem_tex: The figure shows velocity in ft/sec on $0\le t\le6$. The object attains its maximum speed when $t=$
explanation_tex: Speed is $|v|$. The largest magnitude shown is $3$ ft/sec, attained at $t=3$ where $v=-3$.

figure.alt: Velocity on [0,6], with corners at t=1,2,3.

stem_tex: The figure shows velocity in ft/sec on $0\le t\le6$. The speed of the object is increasing during the time interval
explanation_tex: On $(2,3)$ the velocity is negative and becomes more negative. Hence its magnitude, the speed, increases.

figure.alt: Velocity on [0,6], with corners at t=1,2,3.

stem_tex: The figure shows velocity in ft/sec on $0\le t\le6$. The acceleration of the object is positive during the time interval
explanation_tex: Acceleration is the slope of the velocity graph. The only segment with positive slope is $(3,6)$.

figure.alt: Velocity on [0,6], with corners at t=1,2,3.

stem_tex: The figure shows velocity in ft/sec on $0\le t\le6$. How many times on $0<t<6$ is the object's acceleration undefined?
explanation_tex: The velocity graph has corners at $t=1,2,3$, where the one-sided slopes differ. Acceleration is undefined at these three times.

figure.alt: Velocity on [0,6], with corners at t=1,2,3.

stem_tex: The figure shows velocity in ft/sec on $0\le t\le6$. During $2<t<3$, the object's acceleration (in ft/sec$^2$) is
explanation_tex: Acceleration is the slope of velocity. On this segment, $a=[v(3)-v(2)]/(3-2)=(-3-0)/1=-3$ ft/sec$^2$.

figure.alt: Velocity on [0,6], with corners at t=1,2,3.

resolved_source_issue: From the graph, $v(2)=0$ and $v(3)=-3$. The slope on $(2,3)$ is $(-3-0)/(3-2)=-3$ ft/sec$^2$, which is absent from the choices.

stem_tex: The figure shows velocity in ft/sec on $0\le t\le6$. The object is farthest to the right when $t=$
explanation_tex: Velocity is positive before $t=2$ and negative after it. Position therefore increases to $t=2$ and then decreases, so the object is farthest right at $t=2$.

figure.alt: Velocity on [0,6], with corners at t=1,2,3.

stem_tex: The figure shows velocity in ft/sec on $0\le t\le6$. The object's average acceleration (in ft/sec$^2$) for the interval $0 \leq t \leq 3$ is
explanation_tex: The graph gives $v(0)=1.5$ and $v(3)=-3$. Average acceleration is $[v(3)-v(0)]/3=(-3-1.5)/3=-1.5$ ft/sec$^2$.

figure.alt: Velocity on [0,6], with corners at t=1,2,3.

resolved_source_issue: The graph gives $v(0)=1.5$ and $v(3)=-3$. Average acceleration is $(-3-1.5)/3=-1.5$ ft/sec$^2$, which is absent from the choices.
source_correction: Replaced option D with the average acceleration determined by the graph.

stem_tex: The line $y=12x+k$ is tangent to the curve $y=x^3$ when $k$ is equal to
explanation_tex: Tangency requires $3x^2=12$, so $x=\pm2$. Then $k=x^3-12x$ equals $-16$ or $16$.

stem_tex: The two tangents that can be drawn from the point $(4,7)$ to the parabola $y=x^2$ have slopes
explanation_tex: The tangent at $x=a$ is $y=2ax-a^2$. Passing through $(4,7)$ requires $a^2-8a+7=0$, so $a=1,7$. The slopes are $2a=2,14$.

stem_tex: The table shows the velocity at various times of an object moving along a line. An estimate of its acceleration (in ft/sec$^2$) at $t=1$ is $\begin{array}{c|rrrr}t\ (\mathrm{sec})&1.0&1.5&2.1&2.5\\v\ (\mathrm{ft/sec})&10.0&10.8&11.28&11.5\end{array}$
explanation_tex: Use the nearest forward secant: $(10.8-10.0)/(1.5-1.0)=1.6$ ft/sec$^2$.

stem_tex: For $0<x<5$, $f\prime(x)=x\sin x-2\cos x$. $f$ has a local maximum when $x$ is approximately
explanation_tex: Solve $x\sin x-2\cos x=0$ numerically on $(0,5)$: roots are about $1.076874$ and $3.643597$. The derivative changes from positive to negative at the second root, so the local maximum is near $3.644$.

stem_tex: For $0<x<5$, $f\prime(x)=x\sin x-2\cos x$. The graph of $f$ has a point of inflection when $x$ is approximately
explanation_tex: Differentiate to get $f''=3\sin x+x\cos x$. Its zero on $(0,5)$ is approximately $2.455644$, and it changes sign there. Thus the inflection point is near $2.456$.

stem_tex: A particle has position $x=3t$, $y=6t-t^2$. The particle moves along
explanation_tex: Eliminate $t=x/3$ to obtain $y=2x-x^2/9$, the equation of a parabola.

stem_tex: A particle has position $x=3t$, $y=6t-t^2$. The speed of the particle at any time $t$ is
explanation_tex: The velocity components are $x\prime(t)=3$ and $y\prime(t)=6-2t$. Speed is their Euclidean norm: $\sqrt{3^2+(6-2t)^2}=\sqrt{4t^2-24t+45}$.
resolved_source_issue: Velocity is $\langle3,6-2t\rangle$, so speed is $\sqrt{9+(6-2t)^2}=\sqrt{4t^2-24t+45}$. None of the choices equals this expression.
source_correction: Replaced option B with the correct speed formula.

stem_tex: A particle has position $x=3t$, $y=6t-t^2$. The minimum speed of the particle is
explanation_tex: Speed is $\sqrt{9+(6-2t)^2}\ge3$, with equality at $t=3$. The minimum is3.
resolved_source_issue: The speed $\sqrt{9+(6-2t)^2}$ is minimized at $t=3$ and equals $3$. No choice gives $3$.
source_correction: Replaced option C with the correct minimum speed.

stem_tex: A particle has position $x=3t$, $y=6t-t^2$. The acceleration of the particle
choices_tex: is constant both in magnitude and in direction
explanation_tex: Differentiating position twice gives acceleration $\langle0,-2\rangle$, constant in both magnitude and direction.

stem_tex: If a particle moves along a curve with constant speed, then
choices_tex: the magnitude of its acceleration must equal zero
the direction of acceleration must be constant
the curve along which the particle moves must be a straight line
its velocity and acceleration vectors must be perpendicular
explanation_tex: Constant speed implies $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf v$ is constant. Differentiating gives $2\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a=0$, so the velocity and acceleration vectors are orthogonal.

stem_tex: A particle is moving on the curve of $y = 3x - \ln x$ so that $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = -3$ at all times $t$. At the point $(1,3)$, $\dfrac{dy}{dt}$ is
explanation_tex: By the chain rule, $dy/dt=(3-1/x)\,dx/dt$. At $x=1$, this is $(3-1)(-3)=-6$.

stem_tex: A particle moves on $r=8\cos2\theta$, with $d\theta/dt=1/4$ radian/sec when $\theta=\pi/6$. At $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$, find the rate of change (in units per second) of the particle's distance from the origin.
explanation_tex: At $\theta=\pi/6$, $r=4>0$, so distance from the origin is $r$. Then $dr/dt=(-16\sin2\theta)(1/4)=-2\sqrt3$.

stem_tex: A particle moves on $r=8\cos2\theta$, with $d\theta/dt=1/4$ radian/sec when $\theta=\pi/6$. At $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$, what is the horizontal component of the particle's velocity?
explanation_tex: Since $x=r\cos\theta$, $x'=r'\cos\theta-r\sin\theta\,\theta'$. Substitute $r=4$, $r'=-2\sqrt3$, $\theta=\pi/6$, $\theta'=1/4$ to get $-3-1/2=-7/2$.

stem_tex: A vertical circular cylinder has radius $r$ ft and height $h$ ft. If the height and radius both increase at the constant rate of 3 ft/sec, then the rate, in square feet per second, at which the lateral surface area increases is
explanation_tex: Lateral area is $A=2\pi rh$. Product differentiation gives $A'=2\pi(r'h+rh')=6\pi(r+h)$.

stem_tex: A tangent drawn to the parabola $y=9-x^2$ at the point $(2,5)$ forms a right triangle with the coordinate axes. The area of the triangle is
explanation_tex: The tangent slope is $-2(2)=-4$, giving $y=-4x+13$. Its intercepts are $13$ and $13/4$, so the triangle area is $\frac12(13)(13/4)=169/8$.

stem_tex: Two cars are traveling along perpendicular roads, car $A$ at 30 mph and car $B$ at 90 mph. At noon, when car $A$ reaches the intersection, car $B$ is 130 miles away, and moving toward the intersection. At 1 P.M. the rate, in miles per hour, at which the distance between the cars is changing is
explanation_tex: At 1 P.M., distances from the intersection are $x=30$, $y=40$, and separation $d=50$. Differentiating $d^2=x^2+y^2$ gives $d'=(30\cdot30+40(-90))/50=-54$ mph.

stem_tex: Two cars are traveling along perpendicular roads, car $A$ at 30 mph and car $B$ at 90 mph. At noon, when car $A$ reaches the intersection, car $B$ is 130 miles away and moving toward the intersection. If $t$ represents the time, in hours, traveled after noon, then the cars are closest together when $t$ is
explanation_tex: Minimize $d^2=(30t)^2+(130-90t)^2$. Setting its derivative $1800t-180(130-90t)$ to zero yields $18000t=23400$, so $t=1.3$ hours.
